chapters.title: Chapter 3: Salary Structure Meets the Tax Regime

lessons.title: Employer NPS, EPF and the ₹7.5 Lakh Retirement Contribution Cap

children.text: Arvind, a finance director at a listed manufacturer in Mumbai, reads Lesson 1 of this chapter and does the obvious thing: he asks HR to push employer NPS to the full 14% of his ₹30 lakh basic. His employer already puts 12% of basic into PF and ₹1,20,000 into a superannuation fund. Next April, his Form 16 shows ₹1,50,000 of "perquisite" he has never heard of.

He hit the ceiling that every well-paid salaried Indian needs to know about: ₹7,50,000 a year of tax-free employer retirement contributions, across all funds combined. Below it, EPF and NPS are the best structuring tools left. Above it, extra contributions are taxed, stay locked, and keep generating taxable income every year.

body.text: Retirement contributions are tax-efficient up to a ceiling. Above it, you lose the tax benefit but keep the lock-in.

children.text: The three buckets that share one cap

children.text: Employer contributions to three places are added together for the cap: a recognised provident fund (your EPF), NPS, and an approved superannuation fund. Your own employee PF, VPF and personal NPS contributions do not count towards it.

body.label: Annual tax-free limit on employer contributions to PF, NPS and superannuation combined
body.context: Under Section 17 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 17(2)(vii) of the 1961 Act). The excess is a taxable perquisite, and income earned on it is taxed every year as "annual accretion".

body.title: What counts towards the cap?
body.question: Which of these is counted towards the ₹7,50,000 limit?
options: Voluntary PF (VPF) you choose to add
Your employer's contribution to your superannuation fund
NPS contributions you make yourself from your bank account
body.explanation: Only employer contributions count: employer PF, employer NPS and employer superannuation. Your own PF, VPF and self-contributions to NPS are outside this cap, although high employee PF has its own separate interest rule, covered below.

children.text: If your employer puts 12% of basic into PF and 14% into NPS, that is 26% of basic. The cap bites once basic crosses about ₹28.85 lakh a year. With no NPS, PF alone would need a basic of ₹62.5 lakh to breach it.

children.text: For most readers, like Pooja, a product manager with ₹12 lakh basic, the cap is irrelevant. Her ₹1,68,000 of employer NPS at 14% saves ₹52,416 of tax at the 30% slab plus cess, with no perquisite risk. The cap is a problem for senior professionals with a large basic, and for anyone whose employer also funds superannuation.

The ₹1,50,000 excess is added to Arvind's taxable salary. At 30% plus 4% cess, that is ₹46,800 of tax (more if surcharge applies at his income level), and the money still sits locked in NPS or the superannuation fund.

body.title: The annual accretion trap: tax on income from the excess, every year

children.text: The excess contribution is taxed once. Then the interest, dividends or growth earned on it, and on earlier years' excess, is taxed again every year as a perquisite. The Income-tax Rules, 2026 prescribe this formula:

content.caption: TP: taxable accretion this year. PC: this year's excess contribution. PC1 and TP1: excess contributions and taxed accretions from earlier years since 1 April 2020. R: income earned by the fund ÷ average of opening and closing balance.

children.text: The taxable accretion keeps compounding as long as the excess stays invested
Your employer or fund usually computes this and reports it in your Form 16. You rarely need to calculate it yourself, but you do need to know it exists.

body.title: Rahul's excess
body.prompt: Rahul's basic is ₹24,00,000. His employer contributes 12% of basic to PF, 14% of basic to NPS, and ₹1,80,000 to a superannuation fund. What is the taxable perquisite from exceeding the cap?
body.explanation: PF ₹2,88,000 + NPS ₹3,36,000 + superannuation ₹1,80,000 = ₹8,04,000. Excess over ₹7,50,000 = ₹54,000, which is added to his taxable salary.

body.title: Fixing Arvind's structure
body.scenario: Arvind is in the new regime, in the 30% slab. His employer is flexible: any retirement contribution he gives up can be paid as special allowance instead, with CTC unchanged. He wants to maximise tax efficiency and is happy to invest for retirement on his own as well.
body.prompt: How should Arvind restructure his employer contributions, and what should he do with the money freed up?
body.modelAnswer: Bring total employer contributions down to ₹7,50,000. The simplest lever is NPS: with PF at ₹3,60,000 and superannuation at ₹1,20,000, employer NPS should be ₹2,70,000, which is 9% of basic, instead of ₹4,20,000. The ₹1,50,000 he gives up comes back as special allowance, which is taxable, but so was the excess, so his tax is about the same while his money is no longer locked or generating taxable accretion every year. Alternatively, if superannuation offers poor returns or flexibility, he could drop it and keep NPS at up to ₹3,90,000. With the freed-up cash, he can invest in equity mutual funds on Zerodha Coin or elsewhere, where long-term gains above ₹1,25,000 a year are taxed at 12.5% only when he sells, often more efficient than taxable annual accretion.

children.text: A separate rule for high employee PF

The ₹7,50,000 cap is about employer money. There is a second, separate limit on your own contributions: interest on employee PF and VPF contributions above ₹2,50,000 in a year is taxable (₹5,00,000 where the employer does not contribute to the fund). EPFO maintains separate taxable and non-taxable accounts and deducts TDS on the taxable interest.

body.label: Monthly basic at which 12% employee PF crosses ₹2,50,000 a year
body.context: That is an annual basic of about ₹20.83 lakh. VPF brings you there sooner.

body.title: Arvind's own PF
body.prompt: Arvind also contributes 12% of his ₹30,00,000 basic as employee PF. On how much of his yearly contribution will the interest be taxable?
body.explanation: Employee PF = 12% × ₹30,00,000 = ₹3,60,000. Interest on the first ₹2,50,000 stays tax-free. Interest on the remaining ₹1,10,000 (and on that amount as it grows in the taxable account) is taxable every year. At 8.25%, the first year's taxable interest would be roughly ₹4,500, since contributions come in through the year.

body.text: Once you are above ₹2,50,000 of employee PF, adding VPF gives you no tax-free interest on the extra. For many high earners, PPF (fully tax-free interest, ₹1,50,000 a year limit) or equity mutual funds are then a better home for additional savings.

body.text: PFRDA now allows non-government subscribers with a large enough corpus to take up to 80% of their NPS corpus as a lump sum. The tax exemption, however, still covers only 60%. Until tax law is amended, plan on paying slab-rate tax on anything you withdraw above 60%.

body.title: The third bucket
body.textWithBlank: The ₹7,50,000 cap covers employer contributions to provident fund, NPS and approved ___ funds.
body.explanation: Recognised provident fund, NPS and approved superannuation funds share the single ₹7,50,000 annual limit on employer contributions.

cards.definition: Annual limit on tax-free employer contributions to PF, NPS and superannuation combined.
Interest or growth on excess employer contributions, taxed every year as a perquisite.
Up to 14% of basic plus DA in the new regime, 10% in the old regime for private employers, under Section 124.
Interest on employee PF and VPF above ₹2,50,000 a year is taxable.
Withdrawals after 5 years of continuous service are tax-free.
Up to 60% of corpus tax-free. Any additional lump sum is currently taxable.

body.title: Check your retirement contributions this year
steps: Add up employer PF, employer NPS and employer superannuation for the year
If the total is above ₹7,50,000, ask HR to trim NPS or superannuation
If you are below the cap and in the new regime, consider raising employer NPS towards 14% of basic
Check whether your employee PF plus VPF is above ₹2,50,000 a year
Look for "annual accretion" or excess contribution perquisites in your Form 16
Before withdrawing EPF, confirm you have 5 years of continuous service including transfers

body.text: Figures use tax year 2026-27 rules. The annual accretion formula, NPS withdrawal rules and surcharge can materially change outcomes for high earners. This lesson is for education and is not personalised tax, investment or retirement advice.

points: Employer contributions to PF, NPS and superannuation are tax-free only up to ₹7,50,000 a year combined.
The excess is taxed as a perquisite, and income on it is taxed every year as annual accretion.
With 12% PF and 14% NPS, the cap bites once basic crosses about ₹28.85 lakh a year.
Interest on your own PF and VPF contributions above ₹2,50,000 a year is taxable, a separate rule from the employer cap.
EPF is tax-free after 5 years of continuous service. NPS lump sums are tax-free only up to 60% of the corpus.
Below the cap, employer NPS is the best new regime lever. Above it, redirect money to flexible investments instead.
